In terms of radiation in space, and other related conspiracy theories, there are a few things that might help put your mind at ease. First you should know that there are 4 types of radiation, alpha, beta, gamma, and free neutrons.

Alpha particles are positively charged helium nuclei that move with energy determined by the decay process that created/released them. Our understanding of atoms as organized by the periodic table leads us to suspect that we know about basically all decay processes. So we can say with some confidence that we will not see alphas anywhere but at specific energies with any frequency. The end result of these statements is that I nor any professor that taught me, was aware of ANY alpha source that could reliably transmit energy through so much as a sheet of tinfoil or any comparably insignificant shield. All of these get blocked out by your skin, clothing, just about anything. They are only dangerous if you ingest or inhale a source, since this causes the dispersal of the alpha releasing material or any other radioactive material to happen at a cellular level.

Beta radiation is high velocity electrons. These have a bit more penetrating power than alphas. Beta electrons are created and accelerated by decay processes, but also in technologies such as cathode ray tubes, as are found in old televisions. Shields as thick as a centimeter can block out pretty much any naturally occurring source of betas. It is possible to accelerate electrons to enormous energies, which makes their debroglie wavelength very small and their penetrative ability increased. If this is happening outside your spaceship with any frequency, it would be hard not to notice. No astronaut has faced this issue.

'gammas' are packets of electromagnetic energy -- photons with a frequency more than a thousand times greater than light. Its important here to recognize the concept of a 'cross section' -- how big does something look to radiation as it moves through space, this is even more important when discussing neutrons. For gammas, cross section is generally proportional to the size of the nucleus it encounters. The most common large nucleus in the human body is calcium. found in your bones. This is why radiation is associated with bone cancer. Gamma radiation is much more likely to be stopped by a Calcium nucleus than any of the other nuclei you carry around with you. Lead is pretty good at stopping these, and almost anything else is not (with the sort of reliability you would want from a meaningful shield). However, with rocket propulsion systems that have to force their way through an atmosphere, heavy spaceship is worthless spaceship, and I don't know of any substantive lead shielding built into the ones we say we use. So this is the principle risk factor people worry about in space travel.

Secondly, we live around radiation all the time, and the notion of the hormesis effect is attested to by more than quacks. I even looked at a study that showed dock workers who dealt regularly with low levels of radiation lived substantially longer on the average than their contemporaries who did not, although I couldn't find that paper today. We most commonly increase our exposure when in flying airplanes. We measure this if by no other means than by flight attendants not constantly dropping dead, and also with instruments that are more precise. We also make these measurements in space. If solar activity is normal, the rates of radiation are not problematic. Spending 2 weeks going to the moon is probably not appreciably different in terms of exposure, with normal solar activity, than spending a few months in an airplane. If regular rates of solar radiation in space were lethal to humans on the time scale of days or weeks, due to what radiation does to all matter (its an equal opportunity ionizer), it would also be crippling to any sort of satellite launched into space that isn't coated in inches of lead. We don't have to do this, and satellites last for decades.
